script: What would you do if the family that threw you away came back the moment you got rich? My name doesn't matter, but my story does. When I was sixteen, my stepdad told my mom it was him or me, and she chose him. I spent that Christmas in a shelter while my little sister opened presents I used to buy her. Nobody called. Not on my birthday, not when I graduated, not when I got into college on a scholarship I earned by studying in a public library because I didn't have a desk. For six years, silence. I built a small business from nothing, just me, a laptop, and every ounce of anger I had left. Then a local news segment ran a story about it, and within a week my phone would not stop buzzing. My mom texted first. Miss you so much, sweetheart. Then my stepdad, of all people, called to say family is family. Even my sister, now nineteen, messaged asking if I could help her with tuition, like six years of nothing had just been a rough patch. I didn't reply for two weeks. I let every message sit there unread while I thought about that Christmas in the shelter. Then I invited them all to dinner. They showed up smiling, already talking about how proud they were, already asking about investing in my company. I waited until dessert. Then I slid an envelope across the table. Inside was a printed copy of every unanswered text I sent them for six years, the school notice they never opened, and the shelter intake form with my name on it. I told them the door works both ways, and I finally closed mine. My stepdad's face went white. My mother started crying. I just paid the bill and left. They still don't understand that the money was never the point. The point was they showed up exactly six years too late.
